prompt: A field name in a public API will be used by thousands of customers once released. The team slows down to review it carefully.
tells: used by thousands of customers once released
why: Hard-to-undo choices deserve care and review.
trap: A review may be written, but the cue is irreversibility.

prompt: A migration will drop a database column and its data. The engineer asks for a second reviewer and a backup before running it.
tells: drop a database column and its data
why: Irreversible data changes need extra care and an exit plan.
trap: No incident yet; this is about preventing one.

prompt: The team is about to sign a five-year cloud contract with heavy exit fees. The lead insists on a cost review and a plan to avoid vendor lock-in.
tells: five-year cloud contract with heavy exit fees
why: Costly-to-reverse commitments need slow, careful decisions.
trap: There's a vendor, but the issue is reversibility, not making vs buying.

prompt: In a system design interview, a candidate says the ID format will be stored in every client forever, so they spend extra time choosing it.
why: Call out the decisions that can't be undone.
trap: It's not a question to the interviewer; it's weighing permanence.

prompt: Choosing the language for a platform 40 teams will build on, the architect runs a month of trials and a written review.
tells: a platform 40 teams will build on
why: A choice many depend on is very hard to reverse.
trap: A doc is written, but the reason for care is that it can't easily be undone.

prompt: A script will email all two million customers. The engineer tests it on an internal list and gets a second check first, since a sent email can't be recalled.
tells: a sent email can't be recalled
trap: Testing is part of it, but the cue is permanence.
